what_its_for: Deferoxamine is used to remove excess iron from your body. This can happen when you have received many blood transfusions, have accidentally swallowed too much iron, or have a condition that causes your body to store too much iron. It works like a magnet that grabs onto the extra iron and helps your body get rid of it through your urine and stool.
how_to_take: Deferoxamine is given as an injection under your skin (subcutaneous), into a muscle (intramuscular), or directly into your vein (intravenous). A healthcare provider will usually give you your first dose and teach you how to give it to yourself at home if needed. For ongoing iron overload treatment, it is most often given slowly under the skin using a small pump over 8 to 12 hours, typically overnight while you sleep. Always follow exactly how your doctor or nurse has shown you to give this medicine. Never try to inject it yourself without proper training.
dosing: Your dose depends on your weight, how much extra iron is in your body, and the reason you are being treated. For iron overload from blood transfusions, a common adult dose is 20 to 40 mg per kg of body weight given under the skin over 8 to 12 hours, up to 5 to 7 nights per week. For iron poisoning, higher doses may be given directly into a vein in a hospital. Your doctor will check your iron levels regularly and adjust your dose as needed. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a scheduled infusion or injection, give it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or give two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for advice.
storage: Store unopened vials of deferoxamine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from light and moisture. After mixing the powder with sterile water to prepare the injection, use it right away or store it in the refrigerator and use within 24 hours. Do not freeze the mixed solution. Keep all medicines out of reach of children. Throw away any unused or expired medicine properly — ask your pharmacist how to dispose of it safely.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking high-dose vitamin C supplements (more than 200 mg per day) unless your doctor tells you it is okay, as this can cause heart problems when taken with deferoxamine. Avoid driving or using heavy machinery if this medicine makes you feel dizzy or affects your vision or hearing. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as some medicines can interact with deferoxamine. Avoid alcohol as it may increase the risk of side effects.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden vision changes or loss of vision; hearing loss or ringing in your ears; trouble breathing or shortness of breath; chest pain or fast heartbeat; signs of infection at the injection site such as redness, swelling, warmth, or discharge; fever, chills, or feeling very unwell; severe skin rash or allergic reaction (hives, swelling of face or throat, difficulty breathing); pain in your legs or joints; dark reddish-brown or very orange-colored urine (this can be normal but tell your doctor if you are unsure); signs of low blood pressure such as dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting.
when_it_works: You may notice your urine turns a reddish-brown or orange color — this is normal and is a sign the medicine is working to remove iron from your body. It may take several weeks to months of regular treatment before your iron levels come down to a safe range. Your doctor will check your blood and iron levels regularly to see how well the treatment is working. Do not stop using this medicine without talking to your doctor, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Children: Deferoxamine is used in children, but the dose is carefully calculated based on weight. Children should be monitored closely for effects on growth and bone development. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. This medicine should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed and the benefits outweigh the risks. Breastfeeding: It is not known if deferoxamine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney problems: Use with caution if you have kidney problems, as this medicine is removed from the body through the kidneys. Elderly: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects and should be monitored closely by their doctor.
